title: Distribution of aerophilous diatom communities associated with terrestrial green macroalgae in the South Shetland Islands, Maritime  Antarctica - PROTOCOL
author: Juliana Ferreira da Silva

steps_raw.instruction: During the Brazilian Antarctic expeditions the group participated, at the sampling points were collected portions of Prasiola crispa, approximately 100g, and stored in zip bag identified. These bags were frozen for further processing of the material at the Antarctic Vegetation Studies Center and Ficology Laboratory. An aliquot of P. crispa was observed under an optical microscope immediately after sampling (whenever possible) to visualize the community before oxidation.

To prepare the material, cell contents and organic matter of the samples were removed by oxidation with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and potassium permanganate (KMnO4) for a week, during this period we change the hydrogen peroxide daily, samples are heated for best oxidation result. After washing with distilled water, permanent slides were mounted using Naphrax (refractive index of 1.74, Brunel Microscopes Ltd, Chippenham, Wiltshire, United Kingdom). Qualitative and quantitative analyses were carried out under light microscopy (LM) with a 100X in Leica DM750 optical microscope. Samples selected for scanning electron microscopy analysis were filtrated through polycarbonate membrane filters with a pore diameter of 3 µm, mounted on stubs, sputtered with platinum using a BAL–TEC MED 020 Modular High Vacuum Coating System for 30 seconds at 100 mA and studied with scanning electron microscope Hitachi SU–70 (Hitachi High-Technologies Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) operated at 5 kV and 10 mm distance.

The quantitative analysis was performed with approximately 80 valves for each sample, because the abundance is very small in this substrate. It was necessary to make a lot of permanent slides to observe near this amount. Taxa were identified with specific bibliography of Antarctic diatoms.

The spatial distance in meters between each pair of sampling sites was calculated based on the registered geographical points. A geographic distance matrix was constructed for further comparison with the matrices from biological similarity of relative abundance (abundance of individuals by taxa) and species composition (presence and absence of taxa in points).

The estimation of species richness was based on the simple arithmetic of the estimators, without considering their standard deviations (Filgueiras et al. 2016). The sample sufficiency was calculated based on the percentage of values ​​observed in relation to the estimated values. In order to compare the species richness among the sample points, individual rarefaction curves were constructed, and compared in the lowest abundance value among them (N = 41), in order to correct differences in size and sample effort. For this purpose, the abundance data of each species were used for each sampling point. The EstimateS program (Department of Ecology & Evolutionary Biology, University of Connecticut, Storrs, USA) was used for these analyzes, with 100 randomisations of the data (Colwell 2013). Rank-abundance diagrams were constructed to describe and compare the distribution of abundance and dominance of species at each sampling site using relative abundance data (Bitencourt and Da Silva 2016). To describe these distributions numerically, the Pielou equitability index was adopted, based on the Shannon diversity index.

The diversity was partitioned into the alpha, beta and gamma components using Hill's numbers (Jost 2006, 2007) with the “entropart” package (Marcon and Herault 2014) of the R program (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) (R Core Team 2017), with the approach of multiplicative partitioning of diversity.

Jaccard and Bray-Curtis dissimilarity coefficients were used to calculate dissimilarity between pairs of sampling points based on incidence and abundance data. An array of geographical (Euclidean) distances between points was derived from the longitude and latitude coordinates. Subsequently, the Jaccard and Bray-Curtis distance matrices were regressed with the geographic distance matrix using linear regressions (Manly 1997).

The standard coefficients of these regression models will be used as measures of the decay rate in the similarity as a function of the geographical distance between points (Wetzel et al. 2012). In addition, biotic distance data were correlated with the geographic distance matrix in order to corroborate the relationship probability values based on 10.000 permutations using the Mantel test (Goldenberg Vilar et al. 2014). Statistical analyzes were performed in the R program using the "vegan" packages (Oksanen et al. 2016) and "betapart" (Baselga 2010) visually shown through dendrograms also using the "vegan" package (Oksanen et al. 2016) in R.

In order to verify which component of the beta diversity mostly contributed to the dissimilarity between sampling points, species presence/absence dissimilarity was decomposed into substitution (turnover) and nestedness (Baselga 2010) components, while abundance based dissimilarity was decomposed into the components of abundance balanced variation and abundance gradients (Baselga 2013). For this, Jaccard and Bray-Curtis dissimilarity coefficients were used on the "betapart" package (Baselga and Orme 2012) of the R program. The matrices of beta diversity components based on presence / absence and abundance were also associated to the geographic distance matrix, as previously described, in order to verify which dissimilarity component was related to the spatial configuration of the sampling sites.
